I am seventy-six years old, and I have worked my land in Quzhou County since I was a girl. My mother taught me how to read the sky and feel the soil, and though I only finished primary school, I know these fields better than any book. My back is bent now, and my son comes from the city to help with the machine work, but the decisions are still mine.

This year I will plant winter wheat on my five mu in early October, just after the National Day holiday. I will use an improved variety—wheat is not hybrid, but the new seeds from the shop yield better than what my grandmother saved. Before sowing, I will hire the rotary tiller to break and smooth the soil; wheat needs a soft bed to germinate. I will spread one hundred jin of compound fertilizer as a basal dose, and in the spring when the wheat greens up, I will topdress with urea. Water is the lifeblood here, so I will irrigate three times: after sowing, once in winter if the drought is cruel, and once at the jointing stage. The aphids and grassy weeds always come, so I will spray three times—herbicide once and insecticide twice. I expect about one thousand jin per mu if the weather is kind.

In early June, when the wheat turns golden, I will harvest it and immediately plant summer maize in the same fields the same week. There is no time to waste in the double-cropping system of the North China Plain. For maize, I buy hybrid seed from the agricultural supply shop—Denghai or Nongda, one package per mu—because hybrids resist disease and give the yield I need to live. I do not till the land for maize anymore; we sow directly into the wheat stubble with the no-till machine. This saves diesel, time, and my old bones. I apply compound fertilizer at planting, irrigate twice—once when the plants are knee-high and once at tasseling if the rains fail—and spray three times for borers and weeds. I hope for eleven hundred jin per mu.

I keep two hundred jin of wheat for my own flour and dumplings; the rest I sell to the grain station. All the maize goes to the market or the feed mill. I do not grow cotton or vegetables anymore—I am too old for the bending and pruning, and their prices jump like frightened rabbits. Wheat and maize are safe. The government gives us grain subsidies, the buyers are honest, and I have grown these crops for sixty years. They are like family to me.
